slides.0.title: Red grape varieties
slides.0.subtitle: Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent
slides.1.title: The share of reds and the leading variety
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Reds are about one third
slides.1.highlights.0.content: About 32% of the 2022 area was red (wein.plus); other sources put red at about 30% of wine produced — the basis of the statistic differs
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Zweigelt
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The most widely planted red variety (about 13.4% of the area in 2025)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Zweigelt's parentage
slides.1.highlights.2.content: A cross of St. Laurent × Blaufränkisch, bred by Friedrich Zweigelt at Klosterneuburg in 1922
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Style
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Juicy cherry and black cherry with spice; soft tannins, from light to oaked
slides.1.content: Zweigelt = St. Laurent and Blaufränkisch as parents — a favourite exam question.
slides.2.title: Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Blaufränkisch
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Burgenland's flagship red (about 5.8% in 2025): dark berries, pepper and spice with firm acidity and tannin
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Key regions
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The Mittelburgenland, Leithaberg and Eisenberg DACs centre on Blaufränkisch
slides.2.highlights.2.title: St. Laurent
slides.2.highlights.2.content: A silky, aromatic native red often compared with Pinot Noir; harder to grow
slides.2.content: Blaufränkisch = firm, spicy, mineral; Zweigelt = soft and juicy.
slides.3.title: Other reds
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Blauburger and Blauer Portugieser
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Blauburger and Zweigelt together make up nearly half of the red wine (Wikipedia); Portugieser is light and soft
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Pinot Noir (Blauburgunder)
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Delicate expressions in places such as the Thermenregion, Burgenland and Wagram
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Blauer Wildbacher
slides.3.highlights.2.content: The grape of Weststeiermark's rosé Schilcher, with very high acidity
slides.3.highlights.3.title: International varieties
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah are often used in Burgenland blends
slides.3.content: Master Zweigelt, Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent first, then the rest.
slides.4.title: Red styles and regions
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Neusiedlersee
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Zweigelt is bottled as Neusiedlersee DAC and Reserve, rich in fruit
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Carnuntum
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Known for Zweigelt, also Blaufränkisch and blends
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Mittelburgenland
slides.4.content: Level 2 covers the DAC details.
slides.5.title: Diploma depth: red-variety debates and the shift in style
slides.5.highlights.0.title: Zweigelt was first called Rotburger
slides.5.highlights.0.content: The variety was bred as Rotburger and renamed after its breeder Friedrich Zweigelt only in 1975. Because of his role in the Nazi era, there have been recent calls to revert to Rotburger; for exams, know the original name and the parentage
slides.5.highlights.1.title: Blaufränkisch synonyms
slides.5.highlights.1.content: Lemberger in Germany, Kékfrankos in Hungary. Late-ripening and high in acid, it needs warm sites to ripen fully, hence its concentration in Burgenland; in cool years it can taste sharp and green
slides.5.highlights.2.title: From new oak to large casks: a style shift (trend)
slides.5.highlights.2.content: In the 1990s much Blaufränkisch followed an international style of heavy extraction and new barriques; leading producers have since moved to larger, older casks, gentler extraction and earlier picking, stressing acidity, spice and soil (schist in Eisenberg, limestone in Leithaberg). A common trade description: a trend
slides.5.highlights.3.title: Why St. Laurent is hard to grow
slides.5.highlights.3.content: St. Laurent buds early (frost-prone), has thin skins (disease-prone) and irregular yields, so plantings are small; when it succeeds it has a Pinot Noir-like finesse. Use it in essays as an example of “quality potential vs viticultural risk”
slides.5.content: A common red-wine question is “why Burgenland?”: late varieties need Pannonian warmth.
Bred by Friedrich Zweigelt at Klosterneuburg in 1922.
Which is Austria's most widely planted red variety?
Zweigelt is the most planted red, followed by Blaufränkisch.
Which variety makes Weststeiermark's rosé Schilcher?
Schilcher is made from Blauer Wildbacher, with very high acidity.
